displayQuote: To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing

meta.title: Who really said "To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Martin Luther King Jr.: no source before a 1979 devotional. The nearest documented line is Martin Luther's — and his image was a pulse, not breathing.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing'?
meta.ogDescription: Two men named Martin Luther, and a sentence nobody has traced to either. No King source exists; Luther's nearest real line compares prayer to a pulse.

answer.label: No documented author — nearest genuine voice
answer.authorDates: 1483–1546 · German theologian & leader of the Protestant Reformation
answer.sourceLine: No sermon, speech, book or paper of King’s has ever been produced for this sentence; English Wikiquote files it under Disputed, with nothing in print earlier than a 1979 Moody Press devotional — eleven years after King was killed in 1968. The nearest documented line is Martin Luther’s: preaching on John 14 in 1537–38 he compared the praying Christian to a body with a pulse. But a pulse is not breathing, this exact wording appears in none of Luther’s works either, and no one has traced the popular sentence back to him.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Martin Luther King Jr. — no supporting source located
Sermons on the Gospel of St. John, Chapters 14–16 (1537–38)
J. Sandys Stanyon, revised by R. W. Stewart (Williams & Norgate, 1906)
George Sweeting, Talking It Over (Moody Press, 1979), p. 88 — the earliest Wikiquote points to

source.excerpt: Therefore, where there is a Christian, there is also the Holy Ghost, and He does nothing else save pray continually. For even if the mouth be not always moving and uttering words, yet the heart goes on beating unceasingly with sighs like these: Ah! dear Father, may Thy name be hallowed, may Thy kingdom come, and Thy will be done; and whenever there come sorer buffetings and trials and needs, then the sighing and supplication increase, even audibly, so that you cannot find a Christian who does not pray; just as you cannot find a living man without a pulse that never stands still, but beats and beats on continually of itself, although the man may sleep or do anything else, so being all unconscious of this pulse.
trail: English Wikiquote files this line under Disputed on its Martin Luther King Jr. page ↗, citing George Sweeting’s Talking It Over (1 Sep 1979), p. 88 and The Basics of the Christian Life (1 Aug 1983), p. 83, and adding: “No earlier sources are pointed out.”

Asked in October 2010 whether the line belonged to King or to the reformer, Luther-quote researcher James Swan replied that he could find only “something very similar” ↗ — a passage he traced through WA 45 to Luther’s comments on John 14, cited as LW 24:89.

That passage was already circulating in English by 1906, printed in Wilhelm Herrmann’s The Communion of the Christian with God ↗ at pp. 331–332 — and the comparison there is to a pulse, not to breathing.

King did preach on prayer. The King Papers’ sermon “The Misuse of Prayer” ↗ opens by calling prayer “as natural to the human organism as the rising of the sun is to the cosmic order” — a different analogy, and the breathing sentence appears nowhere in it.
source.excerptNote: Luther on John 14, as printed in the 1906 English translation of Wilhelm Herrmann’s The Communion of the Christian with God at pp. 331–332, where it is footnoted to the Erlangen edition (xlix. 115) at p. 332. The modern Luther’s Works translation renders the closing comparison “just as impossible as a living person without a pulse.” Neither version says “breathing.”

source.rightsNote: The popular “breathing” sentence has no located author and no printing earlier than a 1979 devotional, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The Luther passage quoted above is shown in J. Sandys Stanyon’s English translation as revised by R. W. Stewart (Williams & Norgate, 1906), which is public domain in the United States; the modern rendering in Luther’s Works vol. 24, translated by Martin H. Bertram for Concordia Publishing House, is a later translation still under copyright.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: Who Martin Luther was
author.metaLine: 1483–1546 · German theologian & leader of the Protestant Reformation
author.bio: Martin Luther was a German Augustinian friar who became professor of theology at Wittenberg; his 1517 protest against indulgences split Western Christianity and set off the Reformation. He preached and wrote at enormous volume and translated the Bible into German, and it is in his sermons on the Gospel of John, delivered in 1537–38, that the prayer-as-heartbeat image appears. He is a wholly different person from Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968), the American civil-rights leader born four centuries later.

copyAttribution: "To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing." — not Martin Luther King Jr. Nothing in his sermons, speeches or papers contains it; Wikiquote lists it as disputed, and the earliest printing located is George Sweeting, Talking It Over (Moody Press, 1979), p. 88 — eleven years after King's death in 1968. The nearest documented line is Martin Luther's: preaching on John 14 in 1537–38 he said you cannot find a Christian who does not pray, "just as you cannot find a living man without a pulse" — a pulse, not breathing, and nobody has traced the popular sentence back to him.

misattribution.heading: Two Martin Luthers, one improved metaphor
misattribution.intro: Both credits in circulation for this sentence are wrong, and they are wrong in different ways. One man never said it at all; the other said something adjacent, with a different organ.

items.why: Quote databases, sermon slides and greeting cards put the line in King’s mouth, but no speech, sermon, book or paper of his has ever been produced for it. English Wikiquote lists it under Disputed ↗ with nothing earlier than George Sweeting’s Talking It Over (1979) — eleven years after King was killed in 1968.

Many sites hand the line to the reformer instead. He did preach that you cannot find a Christian who does not pray, “just as you cannot find a living man without a pulse” — in his 1537–38 sermons on John 14–16, traced by James Swan to WA 45 / LW 24:89 ↗. But a pulse is not breathing, and the sentence as quoted appears in none of his works.

misattribution.truthLine: The nearest documented line is Martin Luther’s, and its image is a heartbeat — though nobody has traced the breathing sentence back to it. The tidy sentence about breathing belongs to neither Martin Luther nor Martin Luther King Jr.: the earliest printing anyone has produced is George Sweeting’s 1979 Moody Press devotional ↗.

context.heading: Why this one drifts
lead: The confusion is baked into the name. Martin Luther, the sixteenth-century German reformer, and Martin Luther King Jr., the twentieth-century American civil-rights leader, are separated by four centuries and by almost everything else — yet they sit side by side in quotation databases, and lines slide freely between them. This one has been sliding for decades: the same sentence is published as King’s on some sites and as Luther’s on others.

What the two have in common is the analogy — though nobody has actually joined them up. Preaching on John 14, Luther argued that prayer in a Christian is involuntary and continuous, going on beneath speech the way the pulse goes on beneath sleep. The popular sentence puts breath where Luther put a pulse — which reads better on a poster, and quietly loses his actual point, that the praying happens whether or not you are aware of it. But no one has traced whether the breathing version descends from the sermon at all, or where it was first written.
context.detailsSummary: Why “no earlier source” is decisive here
detailsBody: King died on 4 April 1968. The earliest printing anyone has produced for this sentence is George Sweeting’s Talking It Over, published by Moody Press in 1979 — eleven years later — and Wikiquote records flatly that no earlier source has been pointed out. For a man whose sermons, speeches and papers are among the most exhaustively edited bodies of twentieth-century American writing, an eleven-year gap with nothing before it is close to decisive.

The Luther evidence runs the other way, which is what makes the contrast useful. The pulse passage is locatable in the standard editions — traced to WA 45 and printed as Luther’s Works 24:89 — and it was already circulating in English translation by 1906. That is what a real attribution looks like, and it is precisely what the breathing version lacks.
context.pull: Luther’s image was a pulse — something the body does while you sleep. Breathing you can hold.
